Private search company DuckDuckGo has published a new survey revealing how much personal information people share with AI chatbots—and how little many understand about where those conversations go. Here's what it found.

Survey shows AI users share more than they realize

DuckDuckGo's survey, published today, highlights several issues around how people use AI chatbots in relation to privacy—including the fact that nearly one-third of users have told an AI something they wouldn't tell a friend, family member, colleague, or medical professional. Among those who self-identify as AI enthusiasts, that figure rises to 56%.

Here's what DuckDuckGo had to say:

The company says that of the roughly 2,000 U.S. adults who responded to the survey, 53% don't know or aren't sure that most chatbots use conversations for training by default, while only 25% are aware that AI conversations can be subpoenaed by law enforcement.

The results also reveal a clear behavioral divide between parents and non-parents, with parents or guardians in households with children nearly twice as likely to confide in an AI. DuckDuckGo says that "43% of parents using AI have told an AI something they've never told anyone else," while "among AI users without children at home, that number drops to 25%."

DuckDuckGo argues that AI companies have—through advertising campaigns and media appearances—encouraged users to treat chatbots as confidants, even though those conversations may not be as private as users believe.

When it comes to trust, the survey finds people are slightly more confident in large AI companies than in the U.S. government to protect their data. However, both are viewed with significant suspicion: 39% say they don't trust big AI companies at all, compared to 48% who feel the same about the government.

Finally, DuckDuckGo argues that users still have a chance to change how they approach AI privacy, especially since chatbot usage habits are still in a relatively early stage:

"When we talk about online privacy with search engines and browsers, a lot of people think, 'It's too late, my data is already out there.' But the most valuable data you share with big tech companies is what you're going to ask next—not what you asked days, months, or years ago. So it's never too late to switch to more privacy-focused online services."

The company also reminds users that there are proactive steps they can take to protect their privacy when using AI chatbots, including choosing services with clearer and more transparent data-handling policies.
